Question_text: Two small tugboats are pulling a large ship in a harbour. Fig. 1.1 represents the view from above and shows the directions of the forces on the ship. Each of the tugboats is exerting a force of 49 kN on the ship.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a top-down view of a large ship being pulled by two tugboats. The ship is an elongated oval shape. Two tugboats are shown, one on each side of the ship, slightly behind its mid-point. Each tugboat is connected to the ship by a dashed line, representing the force. The forces are 49 kN each. The angles of these forces are shown as 20 degrees relative to a central dashed line extending from the ship's rear. The diagram is labeled 'ship' and 'tugboats' and indicates 'not to scale'.

Parts.part_text: Determine by a graphical method the resultant of these two forces and state the scale used.

The engines of the ship are not operating and the water in the harbour is stationary. The ship is moving in a straight line in the direction of the total force exerted by the tugboats. It is travelling at a constant speed. Explain, in terms of the forces acting, why the ship is moving in a straight line at constant speed.

Question_text: A force applied to a solid object may cause it to accelerate so that its velocity changes.

Parts.part_text: State two other properties of the object which may change when a force is applied.
The gravitational field strength g is 10N/kg. Calculate the weight of the spring.

The spring is suspended vertically and a load is attached to its lower end. The spring extends by 2.7cm and does not pass the limit of proportionality. Fig. 2.1 shows the spring and load attached to the lower end of a second identical spring. Suggest one reason why the extension of the second spring differs from 2.7 cm.

State the form of energy stored in the stretched springs.
The load is released and it moves upwards and downwards. The distance travelled in each movement decreases until the load stops moving. Explain why the load stops moving.

Question_text: A solid, rectangular concrete block is lying horizontally on flat ground with one of its largest sides in contact with the ground. Fig. 3.1 shows the dimensions of the block. The weight of the block is 240 N.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the pressure on the ground caused by the block.
State why the total pressure on the ground underneath the block is larger than the value obtained in (a).
State the height of the centre of mass of the block above the ground.

Question_text: A 75W filament lamp in an office is accidentally left switched on for 63 hours when the office is closed.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the electrical energy that is supplied to this lamp in this time.
The efficiency of the lamp is 0.12 (12%). Calculate the energy released by the lamp in the form of light.
The power station that generates the electricity supplied to the office uses oil as its fuel. State and explain whether oil is a renewable or a non-renewable source of energy.
Discuss one environmental consequence of using oil as a source of energy.

Parts.part_text: Discuss the process of nuclear fusion taking place in the Sun.

Question_text: Fig. 6.1 shows a girl standing a few hundred metres in front of a large building. The girl uses a signal generator and a loudspeaker to send a short pulse of sound towards the building. The sound has a frequency of 3700 Hz. A short time later, the girl hears an echo.
image: Fig. 6.1 shows a girl standing a few hundred metres away from a large multi-story building. The girl is holding a device which appears to be a signal generator and loudspeaker, emitting sound towards the building. The diagram is labeled 'not to scale'.

Parts.part_text: State what is meant by the term echo.
The pitch of the echo is the same as that of the original sound but the echo is not as loud. State what has happened to
the amplitude of the sound wave,
the frequency of the sound wave.
The speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of this sound.

Question_text: A 4.5V battery is connected in a circuit with an ammeter, a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a 1800Ω fixed resistor. Fig. 7.1 is the circuit diagram.
image: Fig. 7.1 shows a series electrical circuit diagram. A 4.5 V battery is connected to an ammeter (labeled 'A'), a 1800 Ω fixed resistor, and a light-dependent resistor (LDR) in series. The LDR is represented by a resistor symbol with an arrow pointing towards it, indicating light dependency.

the total resistance of the circuit,
the reading on the ammeter.

the current in the LDR,
the current in the 1800Ω resistor.

Question_text: In the engine compartment of a car, the battery supplies a current of 120A to the starter motor.

Parts.part_text: The starter motor is switched on for 3.5 s. Calculate the charge that passes through the starter motor in this time.

The starter motor circuit is switched on and off using a relay. The relay is controlled using a second circuit. A switch in the second circuit is used by the driver to operate the relay and turn the starter motor on and off. Explain how the current in the second circuit controls the relay.

Question_text: Fig. 9.1 shows an astronaut in space near to a space station in orbit above the Earth. The total mass of the astronaut and all his equipment is 160 kg. the speed at which the astronaut is travelling after 1.2s.

Parts.part_text: Describe how the distance moved by the astronaut during the first 3.0s may be found using the speed-time graph.

A force acts on the space station to keep it in this orbit.

Explain what causes this force.

Question_text: A boiler containing water is plugged into a 230 V mains supply. The heater in the boiler is operating at full power.

Parts.part_text: The power used by the heater is 2.8kW. Calculate the current in the heater.
The wiring in the cable from the socket and in the boiler remains safe and does not overheat provided that the current is less than 20A. Suggest a suitable fuse rating for the circuit.

The specific heat capacity of water is 4200J/(kg°C). The heater is used to increase the temperature of 6.3 kg of water. In a certain time, the temperature of the water increases from 23°C to 49°C. Calculate the change in the internal energy of the water.

The heater supplies thermal energy to the water at a constant rate. It takes more time for the temperature of the water to increase from 49°C to 75°C than from 23°C to 49°C. In both cases, the increase in temperature is the same. Suggest why it takes more time for the temperature to increase from 49°C to 75°C.
Fig. 10.1 shows the heater at the bottom of the water in the boiler.
Parts.image: Fig. 10.1 shows a cross-section of a boiler. The boiler is a rectangular container made of 'steel'. Inside, 'water' fills most of the container. At the bottom, partially submerged in the water, is a 'heater' element, shown as a coil, connected to an external power source.

Parts.part_text: Explain how thermal energy is transferred from the heater throughout the water.
The part of the boiler that holds the water is made from steel. Describe, in terms of particles, how thermal energy passes through the steel.
State and explain, in terms of particles, what happens to the density of the steel as its temperature increases.
